statement: In adults who chose to attend a ceremony, retreat or other guided session with a classic psychedelic and signed up for online surveys (mostly from Western countries, highly educated, and already leaning towards non-physicalist views beforehand), attending, compared with their own answers about a week before, is associated with modestly stronger agreement with non-physicalist statements 4 weeks and 6 months later; in one randomized trial in depression the shift after psilocybin therapy exceeded the shift after escitalopram only on a one-tailed test; and none of the studies tests whether the beliefs are true. On a questionnaire written for the study, whose main factor groups belief in other realms that can be visited, a unifying principle beyond scientific explanation, panpsychism (mind as a quality of all things), dualism and idealism against materialism and naturalism (Timmermann et al., 2021), the 122 respondents with answers at all three time points (819 in the baseline table and 866 said to have answered at some time point, so about 85 in 100 are missing from these analyses and were not compared with those who stayed) shifted by d = 0.33 at 4 weeks and d = 0.46 at 6 months, and the 53 taking a psychedelic for the first time by d = 0.53 and 0.73; belief in fatalistic determinism rose at 4 weeks (d = 0.25) but not at 6 months. Positions moved both ways: of respondents classed as 'hard materialists' at baseline, 24.4% still held that position at 4 weeks and 22.2% at 6 months, most of the others moving to a mixed position or to dualism, while 17.6% and 15.2% of respondents with mixed positions moved to materialism; of those neutral on panpsychism, 57.3% and 54.5% became 'believers' (group sizes not printed, and the samples behind these tables not stated). In an exploratory path model, feeling emotionally in tune with the group during the session predicted the 4-week score (standardized beta 0.22), while mystical-type and visual-effect scores were dropped as not significant. In the same team's double-blind trial in 59 adults with major depression, a 5-item version of the questionnaire shifted after psilocybin therapy (two 25 mg doses and 6 weeks of daily placebo, study condition; d = 0.45) and less after 6 weeks of daily escitalopram given with two 1 mg doses of psilocybin (d = 0.2, p = 0.33, which the authors call no change); the difference between the arms had p = 0.041 one-tailed, about 0.08 two-sided (editors' calculation). In a retrospective online survey by another team, of 1,606 adults recruited because they attributed a change in their beliefs to a psychedelic experience, each rating 'before', 'after' and 'now' for their most belief-changing experience in one sitting a mean of 8.2 years after it, the share agreeing that plants can be conscious was 26% before against 61% after, fungi 21% against 56%, insects 33% against 57%, rocks 8% against 26% and the universe 34% against 80%, with 'now' close to 'after'; superstitions (black cats bringing bad luck: 8%, 4% and 3%) and belief in free will (74%, 74% and 73%) did not change meaningfully, and people who remembered a more mystical experience reported larger changes (Nayak & Griffiths, 2022). The cohort cannot separate the drug from the ceremony's group, ritual, teaching and expectations, or show that those who stopped answering changed like those who stayed, and its authors say that views held by co-attendees and by the trial's staff may have passed to participants; the survey, recruited on belief change and relying on memory over years, cannot show how often or how much beliefs change. On truth, the first team writes that judging the value of the positions is beyond its work and that it would be hasty to read its results as favouring them, and the second that persistent beliefs after compelling experiences neither support nor undermine their validity. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated by the same team.
plain: Do psychedelics change what people believe about reality? In one study that asked people a week before a psychedelic retreat or ceremony, and again 4 weeks and 6 months after, beliefs moved a little away from 'everything is physical' and towards ideas such as other worlds and a conscious universe, more in first-timers. But only 122 of more than 800 people answered all three times, most already leaned that way, there was no comparison group, and in an exploratory analysis the shift went with feeling in tune with the group rather than with how mystical or visual the trip was. In a small trial in depression, beliefs shifted after psilocybin therapy and a little after a standard antidepressant too, and the difference between them was too small to be sure of. In a survey of people whose beliefs had changed after a psychedelic, looking back about 8 years on average, 26 in 100 remembered believing plants could be conscious before and 61 in 100 after, while superstitions did not rise. None of these studies can say whether the beliefs are true.
population: Adults who planned to attend a retreat, ceremony or other guided experience with a classic psychedelic and signed up at a study website after online advertisements (819 in the baseline table: mean age 44.4; 55.6% men; 43.8% from the United States and 19.5% from the United Kingdom; 90.7% White; 54.1% with a master's, doctoral or professional degree, editors' sum), of whom 122 answered the belief questions at baseline, 4 weeks and 6 months; 59 adults with major depression (30 and 29) in a randomized trial by the same team; and 1,606 adults recruited online by another team because they attributed a change in their beliefs to a psychedelic experience (mean age 35.1; 67% men; 89% White; 69% from the United States).
exposure: Attending a ceremony or retreat with a classic psychedelic (psilocybin mushrooms or truffles, ayahuasca, DMT, San Pedro, LSD or 1P-LSD), the substance, amount and setting chosen by the respondents and not reported; in the trial, psilocybin therapy: 25 mg on two dosing days and 6 weeks of daily placebo (study condition); in the survey, a past experience with psilocybin mushrooms (49%), LSD (33%), ayahuasca (7%), N,N-DMT (6%), 5-MeO-DMT (3%) or mescaline-containing cacti (2%), chosen by each respondent as the one that most changed their beliefs.
comparator: Each respondent's own answers about a week before the ceremony (no comparison group); in the trial, randomized daily escitalopram for 6 weeks with two 1 mg doses of psilocybin; in the survey, respondents' remembered 'before' beliefs, rated in the same sitting as 'after' and 'now'.
outcome: Agreement with non-physicalist statements: a 9-item factor (Cronbach's alpha 0.86) of a 13-item Metaphysical Beliefs Questionnaire written for the study, and 5 of its items in the trial; fatalistic determinism (FAD-Plus items); changes in the position most strongly endorsed; in the survey, the share agreeing that ten kinds of entity can be conscious, five superstition items and one free-will item. Whether any belief is true was not assessed.
magnitude: Timmermann et al. (2021), cohort, 122 with paired data: non-physicalist factor at 4 weeks t(121) = 3.66, Bonferroni p = 0.001, d = 0.33; at 6 months t(121) = 5.07, p < 0.0001, d = 0.46 (the printed 95% CIs [0.12, 0.39] and [0.22, 0.50] cannot be intervals of d; editors' approximate 95% intervals for d, SE = √(1/n + d²/2n), 0.15 to 0.51 and 0.27 to 0.65); first-timers (53): d = 0.53 and 0.73; fatalistic determinism d = 0.25 at 4 weeks (p = 0.012), not at 6 months. Conversion (Figure 2; group sizes not printed): 'hard materialists' remaining 24.4% (4 weeks) and 22.2% (6 months); dualists remaining 55.5% and 65.2%; none/mixed to materialism 17.6% and 15.2%; panpsychism neutral to believer 57.3% and 54.5%, sceptic to believer 22.6% and 37.8%. Lifetime psychedelic use and baseline factor score: Spearman r = 0.223 (cross-sectional). Path model: emotional synchrony to the 4-week score, beta 0.22. Trial (psilocybin therapy 30, escitalopram 29; 5 items): interaction F(56) = 3.13, p = 0.041 one-tailed (editors' calculation: two-sided p = 0.082); psilocybin Z = 2.28, p = 0.02, d = 0.45; escitalopram Z = 0.24, p = 0.33, d = 0.2 (Z = 0.24 gives a one-tailed p of about 0.41, editors' calculation). Nayak & Griffiths (2022), 1,606, % agreeing before, after and now: plants 26, 61, 64; fungi 21, 56, 62; insects 33, 57, 60; inanimate natural objects 8, 26, 29; inanimate man-made objects 3, 15, 17; the universe 34, 80, 82; self 80, 97, 98; no meaningful change for superstitions (black cats 8, 4, 3; Loch Ness monster 10, 10, 10) or free will (74, 74, 73).

risk_of_bias.note: The cohort is at very high risk of bias on its card (ROBINS-E): with no comparison group, the drug cannot be separated from the ceremony's setting, group, ritual, teaching and expectations; about 85 in 100 baseline respondents are missing from the paired analyses, with no comparison of those who stayed and those who left; analytic samples differ between analyses and are not stated; the path model kept significant predictors only; and the questionnaire is new and self-rated, in a culture where the expected direction is familiar. The survey selected respondents on the outcome and asked them to recall earlier beliefs years later (JBI: high risk). The trial is randomized, but its belief items are a 5-item version without reported reliability, analysed secondarily with one-tailed tests, and the paper does not say whether patients could tell their treatment.

inconsistency.note: The direction agrees across the cohort, the trial and the survey (away from materialism, towards panpsychism and wider attribution of consciousness); the conversion tables also show moves towards materialism, which the statement reports. The two papers differ on the role of mystical experience (no link in the cohort's path model, a link in the survey), which the statement also reports.

indirectness.note: Rated as worded, for self-selected ceremony attendees, patients in one trial and survey respondents chosen for a belief change; the statement does not extend the shifts to people who use psychedelics in general.

imprecision.note: The cohort's shifts exclude no change (editors' approximate 95% intervals for d 0.15 to 0.51 at 4 weeks and 0.27 to 0.65 at 6 months); the trial's difference between arms is imprecise (two-sided p about 0.08), which the statement says.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable: no registration or analysis plan is mentioned for the cohort or the survey analyses, and the paper does not say whether the belief items were a registered outcome of the trial.

grade.reasoning: Observational evidence (a prospective cohort without a comparison group and a retrospective survey) starts low; rated down two levels for risk of bias, which is below the floor: very low. Rated as worded: an association between attending a psychedelic ceremony and modest shifts in stated beliefs among people who kept answering; not that psychedelics cause the shift, that it is specific to psychedelics (escitalopram also moved, d = 0.2, and the difference between the arms was significant only one-tailed), or that it lasts beyond 6 months. The trial is randomized and would start high on its own, but as the only comparison between treatments it rests on 59 patients, a 5-item version and a one-tailed p of 0.041 (about 0.08 two-sided), so it qualifies the claim rather than raising it. Status replicated by the same team: the cohort and the trial are one group's two samples, reported in one paper; the survey from another group agrees in direction but recruited people because their beliefs had changed and relied on recall, so it is not counted as an independent test.
